about: Topic guide used by the Ask page. Each topic lists the words that point to it (q), a neutral summary, how each faith sees it, and the key passages grouped by source. A passage is [reference, why it matters]. References are linked and quoted automatically.

topics.title: The Trinity
topics.summary: Christians believe in one God who exists as three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Muslims and Jews believe God is one in a way that rules this out. The word “Trinity” is not in the Bible; Christians use it to sum up what they read there.

views.christian: There is one God, not three. The one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal and eternal. Christians find this in Jesus' command to baptise “in the name” (singular) of all three, in the Gospel of John calling Jesus “the Word” who “was God”, and in the Spirit being spoken of as a person. The Old Testament passages are read as early hints, made clear only after Jesus. The doctrine was put into fixed words at the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).
views.muslim: God is absolutely one (tawhid), with no partner, son or parts. The Quran addresses Christians directly: “say not ‘Three’”, and calls it disbelief to say God is “the third of three”. Jesus is honoured as a prophet and the Messiah, and the Holy Spirit is usually understood as the angel Gabriel. Muslims also point out that Jesus himself quoted “the Lord is one” and that the word Trinity is not in the Bible.
views.jewish: “Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” is the centre of Jewish faith and allows no division in God. The plural in “Let us make man” is explained by Jewish commentators as God speaking to the angels. Worship of a man as God is seen as a breach of the first commandments.

topics.title: Is Jesus God?
topics.summary: Christians believe Jesus is God the Son who became man. Muslims believe he is a great prophet but not God. Jews do not accept him as Messiah or divine. Both sides quote the Gospels.

views.christian: Jesus is fully God and fully man, one person with two natures. He forgave sins, accepted worship and spoke of himself in ways Jews of his time heard as claiming God's authority. The verses where he prays or says “the Father is greater” describe him as a man.
views.muslim: Jesus is a messenger and servant of God, born of a virgin, a worker of miracles, but not God. In the Quran he denies ever asking to be worshipped. Muslims point to the Gospel verses where Jesus prays to God, calls the Father “the only true God”, and does not know the hour.
views.jewish: God has no body and does not become a man. Jesus is not regarded as divine, a prophet or the Messiah.

Jesus is a messenger and a word from God, not God.

topics.title: The crucifixion of Jesus
topics.summary: The New Testament says Jesus was crucified, died and rose again. One verse of the Quran says he was not killed or crucified. Historians generally treat the crucifixion as one of the most certain facts about Jesus.

views.christian: Jesus truly died on the cross for the sins of the world and rose on the third day. Without the cross and resurrection there is no Christianity.
views.muslim: God saved Jesus: he was not killed or crucified but raised to God. Most commentators say someone else was made to look like him and was crucified instead. He will return before the end.
views.jewish: Judaism has no doctrine about Jesus' death. A passage in the Talmud assumes he was executed.

topics.title: The resurrection
topics.summary: Christians believe Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day. All three faiths believe in a resurrection of the dead at the end of time.

views.christian: Jesus rose bodily on the third day and appeared to many witnesses. His resurrection is the promise that believers will also be raised.
views.muslim: Since Jesus was not killed, he did not rise from the dead; he was raised alive to God. All people will be resurrected on the Day of Judgment.
views.jewish: The resurrection of the dead at the end of days is a core belief. Jesus' resurrection is not accepted.

topics.title: The virgin birth
topics.summary: Christians and Muslims both believe Mary conceived Jesus without a man. Jews do not. The prophecy in Isaiah 7:14 is disputed: the Hebrew word means “young woman”.

views.christian: Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, fulfilling Isaiah 7:14.
views.muslim: Mary conceived Jesus by God's command, as a sign. This shows God's power, not that Jesus is God's son: Adam had neither father nor mother.
views.jewish: The virgin birth is not accepted. In Isaiah 7:14 the Hebrew “almah” means a young woman, and the child was a sign for King Ahaz in his own time.

topics.title: Mary, mother of Jesus
topics.summary: Mary is honoured by Christians and Muslims. She is the only woman named in the Quran. Catholics and Orthodox give her special honour; Protestants honour her but do not pray to her.

views.christian: Orthodox and Catholics call her Mother of God and ask for her prayers; Catholics hold she was conceived without sin and taken body and soul into heaven. Protestants honour her as the virgin mother of the Lord but do not pray to her.
views.muslim: Maryam was chosen and purified above the women of the worlds. A whole surah is named after her. She is not divine and is not prayed to.
views.jewish: Mary has no religious role in Judaism.

refs: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.”

topics.title: The Holy Spirit
topics.summary: In Christianity the Holy Spirit is God, the third person of the Trinity. In Islam the Holy Spirit is usually understood as the angel Gabriel. In Judaism the spirit of God is God's presence and power, not a separate person.

views.christian: The Spirit is God, given to the Church at Pentecost. The East says the Spirit proceeds from the Father; the West adds “and the Son”.
views.muslim: “The Holy Spirit” (Ruh al-Qudus) supported Jesus and brought revelation; most scholars identify it with Gabriel. Some Muslims read Jesus' promise of a coming “Comforter” as a prophecy of Muhammad.
views.jewish: The spirit of God is his presence acting in the world and inspiring the prophets, not a person within God.

topics.title: Original sin
topics.summary: Western Christianity teaches that everyone inherits the effects of Adam's sin. Eastern Christians speak of “ancestral sin”. Islam and Judaism say each person is born innocent.

views.christian: Catholics: we inherit the loss of original holiness, removed in baptism. Protestants: the fall corrupted all of human nature. Orthodox: we inherit death and weakness from Adam, not his guilt.
views.muslim: Adam and Eve sinned, repented and were forgiven. Nothing was passed on. Every child is born in a natural state of submission to God (fitra).
views.jewish: No inherited guilt. Each person has a good and an evil inclination and is free to choose.

refs: “In sin did my mother conceive me.”

topics.title: How is a person saved?
topics.summary: Christians say salvation is God's gift through Christ, though they disagree about the role of works. Islam says people are saved by God's mercy through faith and good deeds. Judaism stresses keeping God's commandments and repentance.

views.christian: Protestants: by grace alone, through faith alone; good works are the fruit. Catholics: by grace, received in baptism, lived out in faith working through love. Orthodox: a lifelong union with God (theosis).
views.muslim: Faith in the one God and righteous deeds, weighed on the Day of Judgment, with entry to Paradise only by God's mercy.
views.jewish: Israel is already in covenant with God and is called to keep the commandments and repent when it fails. The righteous of all nations have a share in the World to Come.

topics.title: Heaven, hell and life after death
topics.summary: All three faiths teach a resurrection, a judgment and reward or punishment. They differ on the details, such as purgatory, intercession, and whether punishment lasts for ever.

views.christian: Resurrection and judgment, heaven and hell. Catholics add purgatory, a cleansing for the saved. Protestants reject purgatory. The Orthodox pray for the dead without defining purgatory.
views.muslim: Questioning in the grave, resurrection, the weighing of deeds, the bridge, Paradise and Hell, described in vivid detail in the Quran.
views.jewish: The World to Come and the resurrection of the dead. Judaism focuses more on this life, and punishment after death is usually seen as temporary.

topics.title: The end times and the Day of Judgment
topics.summary: All three faiths expect God to bring history to an end. Christians and Muslims both expect Jesus to return. Jews expect the Messiah's first coming.

views.christian: Jesus will return in glory to judge the living and the dead and make all things new. An Antichrist will oppose him first.
views.muslim: Signs will come before the Hour: the false messiah (Dajjal), the Mahdi, and Jesus descending to defeat the Dajjal. Then resurrection and judgment.
views.jewish: The Messiah, a human king of David's line, will come, gather Israel, rebuild the Temple and bring peace; then the resurrection.

topics.title: The Messiah
topics.summary: Christians believe Jesus is the Messiah foretold by the prophets. Muslims also call Jesus the Messiah, without the Christian meaning. Jews believe the Messiah has not yet come.

views.christian: Jesus fulfilled the prophecies: born in Bethlehem, the suffering servant of Isaiah 53, the king on a donkey. He came first to suffer and will come again to reign.
views.muslim: Jesus is al-Masih, the Messiah, a prophet sent to Israel. The title does not mean he is divine or that he died for sins.
views.jewish: The Messiah will bring universal peace, gather the exiles and rebuild the Temple. This has not happened, so the Messiah has not come. Isaiah's servant is Israel.

topics.title: “Son of God”
topics.summary: For Christians, Jesus is the eternal Son of God. The Quran rejects that God has a son. In the Hebrew Bible, “son of God” is used of Israel, kings and angels.

views.christian: Jesus is the only-begotten Son, eternally one with the Father; believers become God's children by adoption.
views.muslim: God does not beget and is not begotten. Calling anyone God's son is a grave error. Biblical “son of God” language is read as meaning a righteous servant.
views.jewish: “Son of God” describes Israel, the king or the righteous: a relationship, not divinity.

topics.title: Is Muhammad foretold in the Bible?
topics.summary: The Quran says Muhammad is described in the Torah and Gospel. Muslims point to several passages; Christians and Jews read them as being about someone else.

views.christian: The “prophet like Moses” is fulfilled in Jesus. The Comforter is the Holy Spirit. Muhammad is not accepted as a prophet.
views.muslim: The Bible still contains signs of Muhammad: a prophet from the brothers of Israel (the Ishmaelites), the Comforter who will guide into all truth, the servant whom Kedar praises.
views.jewish: Deuteronomy 18 promises prophets from within Israel. Any prophet who changes the Torah is to be rejected.

topics.title: Muhammad
topics.summary: For Muslims, Muhammad is the final prophet and the best example for humanity. Christians and Jews do not accept him as a prophet. His life, as a prophet and ruler, attracts both devotion and criticism.

views.christian: Muhammad is not accepted as a prophet, because the Quran denies the cross and Jesus' divinity, which Christians hold are central.
views.muslim: Muhammad is the seal of the prophets, a mercy to the worlds and the best example of conduct. Muslims explain the criticisms by his historical setting and point to his mercy, justice and reforms.
views.jewish: Not accepted as a prophet, since the Torah given to Moses is not replaced. Medieval Jewish thinkers recognised Islam as strictly monotheistic.

topics.title: Has the Bible been changed?
topics.summary: Many Muslims hold that the Torah and Gospel were altered. Jews and Christians say the text has been faithfully preserved. The manuscripts can be checked, and the Quran itself is read both ways.

views.christian: Bibles from centuries before Islam survive, and they match ours. The Quran tells Christians of its time to judge by the Gospel, which assumes it was reliable. Known variant readings change no doctrine.
views.muslim: God revealed the Torah and the Gospel, but the books Jews and Christians have now are not the original revelations; where they disagree with the Quran, the Quran is the judge.
views.jewish: The Torah is copied by hand under strict rules, and the Dead Sea Scrolls show how carefully the text was handed down.

topics.title: Prayer
topics.summary: Prayer is central to all three faiths. Muslims pray five set prayers a day, Jews three, and Christians have set prayers such as the Lord's Prayer as well as free prayer.

views.christian: Jesus taught the Lord's Prayer and told his followers to pray in secret and without ceasing. Churches also have set daily prayers and the Eucharist.
views.muslim: Five daily prayers facing Mecca, preceded by ritual washing, plus Friday congregational prayer. Shia usually combine them into three times.
views.jewish: Prayer three times a day (morning, afternoon, evening), with the Shema and the Amidah, ideally with a quorum of ten.

refs: Pray in secret; the Lord's Prayer.

topics.title: Fasting
topics.summary: All three faiths fast. Muslims fast from dawn to sunset in Ramadan, Jews fast fully on Yom Kippur, and many Christians fast in Lent and on set days.

views.christian: Jesus fasted forty days and taught his followers to fast without show. Orthodox Christians fast often; Catholics fast in Lent; many Protestants fast privately.
views.muslim: Fasting in Ramadan is one of the five pillars: no food, drink or relations from dawn to sunset, for those who are able.
views.jewish: Yom Kippur is a full 25-hour fast for atonement; there are several other fast days in the year.

topics.title: Charity and the poor
topics.summary: All three faiths command care for the poor. Islam makes alms a pillar of faith, Judaism treats charity as justice, and Jesus warned sharply about wealth.

views.christian: Jesus identified himself with the poor and warned that it is hard for the rich to enter the Kingdom. Christians are to give generously and in secret.
views.muslim: Zakat, a yearly alms of a set share of wealth, is a pillar of Islam. Voluntary charity (sadaqa) and care for orphans are repeatedly commanded.
views.jewish: Tzedakah means justice: giving to the poor is a duty, and Maimonides ranks its highest form as helping someone become self-supporting.

topics.title: Food laws: pork, halal and kosher
topics.summary: Jews keep kosher and Muslims eat halal; both forbid pork. Most Christians hold that the food laws of Moses no longer bind them.

views.christian: Jesus declared all foods clean and the apostles freed non-Jewish believers from the food laws, so most Christians eat pork. Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists, still avoid it.
views.muslim: Pork, blood, carrion, alcohol and meat dedicated to other than God are forbidden. Meat should be slaughtered in God's name (halal). Exceptions apply in necessity.
views.jewish: The Torah's food laws are binding: only certain animals, slaughtered properly, no blood, and no mixing of meat and milk.

refs: Clean and unclean animals; the pig is unclean.

topics.title: Alcohol
topics.summary: Islam forbids alcohol. Judaism and most of Christianity permit wine in moderation and use it in worship, while condemning drunkenness.

views.christian: Wine is permitted and used in the Eucharist; drunkenness is a sin. Some Protestant churches ask members to abstain.
views.muslim: Intoxicants are forbidden. The Quran prohibited them in stages, ending with a clear command to avoid them.
views.jewish: Wine is blessed and used at Sabbath and festivals; drunkenness is condemned.

refs: Do not get drunk with wine.
In wine is great sin and some benefit, but the sin is greater.
Do not approach prayer while intoxicated.
Wine and gambling are the work of Satan; avoid them.

topics.title: The Sabbath and the holy day
topics.summary: Jews keep the Sabbath from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Most Christians worship on Sunday, the day of the resurrection. Muslims gather for prayer on Friday but have no day of rest.

views.christian: Christians gather on Sunday, the Lord's Day, the day Jesus rose. Most hold that the Sabbath law was fulfilled in Christ; some groups keep Saturday.
views.muslim: Friday is the day of congregational prayer; work may resume after it. God needs no rest.
views.jewish: The Sabbath is the seventh day, a sign of the covenant: no work, from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday.

topics.title: The Law of Moses
topics.summary: Judaism says the Torah's commandments bind the Jewish people for ever. Christianity says the law was fulfilled in Christ. Islam says each community was given a law and Muhammad's is final.

views.christian: Jesus fulfilled the law. The moral law, like the Ten Commandments, stands; the ritual and civil laws of ancient Israel do not bind Christians.
views.muslim: God gave the Torah to Moses and later the sharia through Muhammad, which replaces earlier laws while confirming much of them.
views.jewish: The 613 commandments of the Torah are eternal and are lived out through the rabbis' interpretation.

refs: Do not add to it or take from it.

topics.title: Abraham's sacrifice: Isaac or Ishmael?
topics.summary: Genesis says God told Abraham to sacrifice Isaac. The Quran tells the story without naming the son; most Muslims today say it was Ishmael.

views.christian: It was Isaac, a picture of God giving his own Son.
views.muslim: Most Muslims say Ishmael, Abraham's firstborn; the good news of Isaac comes after the story in the Quran. Early scholars were divided.
views.jewish: The binding of Isaac is central to Jewish faith and is read at the New Year.

refs: Ishmael is born when Abraham is 86.

topics.title: Moses
topics.summary: Moses is honoured by all three faiths as the great prophet who led Israel out of Egypt and received the Law. He is the prophet most often mentioned in the Quran.

views.christian: Moses gave the Law; Jesus is the greater prophet and fulfils it.
views.muslim: Musa is one of the greatest messengers, to whom God spoke directly and gave the Torah.
views.jewish: Moses is the greatest of the prophets, through whom the whole Torah was given.

refs: The burning bush and the divine name.
Jesus counted worthy of more glory than Moses.
The law came through Moses; grace and truth through Jesus.

topics.title: Jesus in Islam
q: what does the quran say about jesus
topics.summary: The Quran honours Jesus as the Messiah and a great prophet, born of a virgin, who worked miracles and will return. It denies that he is God or was crucified.

views.christian: Christians welcome the honour Islam gives Jesus but hold that the Quran misses what matters most: that he is God's Son who died and rose for sinners.
views.muslim: Isa is one of the five greatest messengers. He spoke in the cradle, healed the blind and lepers, and raised the dead by God's permission. He was raised to God and will return.
views.jewish: Judaism accepts neither the Christian nor the Islamic claims about Jesus.

refs: Healing the blind and the leper, raising the dead, by God's permission.

Jesus will descend as a just ruler.

topics.title: Jesus in Judaism
topics.summary: Judaism does not accept Jesus as the Messiah, a prophet or divine. Many modern Jewish scholars see him as a Jewish teacher of his time.

views.christian: Jesus fulfilled Israel's scriptures, and the first Christians were Jews who recognised him as Messiah.
views.muslim: Muslims agree with Christians that Jesus was the Messiah and a prophet, but agree with Jews that he was not God.
views.jewish: The Messiah's work, world peace and the ingathering of Israel, has not happened. Worshipping a man is forbidden.

refs: Israel gathered, David's descendant as king, the sanctuary restored.
A prophet who leads astray from the commandments.

topics.title: Paul the apostle
topics.summary: Paul wrote much of the New Testament. Christians see him as a faithful apostle; many Muslims and some scholars argue he changed Jesus' message.

views.christian: Paul preached the same gospel as the other apostles, who accepted him; his letters are scripture.
views.muslim: Many Muslims hold that Paul introduced Jesus' divinity, the atoning death and the setting aside of the law.
views.jewish: Paul is seen as the figure most responsible for Christianity's break with Torah observance.

refs: Paul says his gospel came by revelation.

topics.title: Sunni and Shia
topics.summary: The split began over who should lead the Muslims after Muhammad. Sunnis accepted the elected caliphs; Shia believe Muhammad appointed Ali, followed by Imams from his family.

views.muslim: Sunnis: the community rightly chose Abu Bakr, then Umar, Uthman and Ali; leaders are guardians, not infallible. Shia: the Prophet named Ali at Ghadir Khumm; the twelve Imams are chosen by God and protected from error, and the twelfth will return as the Mahdi.

God wishes to purify you, people of the house.
The Book of Divine Authority on the Imams.

topics.title: The pope and Peter
topics.summary: Catholics believe Jesus made Peter head of the Church and that the popes succeed him. Orthodox and Protestants reject the pope's universal authority.

views.christian: Catholic: Peter is the rock, and the pope holds his office and can define doctrine infallibly. Orthodox: Rome had first place in honour, not rule. Protestant: the rock is Peter's faith or Christ himself, and no successor is mentioned.

refs: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.
Peter calls himself a fellow elder.

topics.title: Scripture and tradition
q: how many books in the bible
topics.summary: Each faith debates whether the written text is enough or needs an authorised tradition beside it. The churches also differ on which books belong in the Old Testament.

views.christian: Protestants: Scripture alone is the final authority, 66 books. Catholics: Scripture and Tradition with the Church's teaching office, 73 books. Orthodox: Scripture within Holy Tradition, with the Septuagint books.
views.muslim: The Quran is read together with the Prophet's example (sunna) recorded in hadith; Sunni and Shia trust different collections.
views.jewish: The written Torah comes with an oral Torah, recorded in the Mishnah and Talmud. Karaites accept the written text alone.

refs: Hold to the traditions, by word or by letter.
Jesus condemns traditions that cancel God's word.
Take what the messenger gives you.
The messenger explains what was sent down.
[[go/trent-canons-and-decrees/Session IV › Canonical Scriptures|Council of Trent on the canon]]

topics.title: Baptism and the sacraments
topics.summary: Christians baptise and celebrate the Lord's Supper, but differ on their meaning. Catholics and Orthodox count seven sacraments; most Protestants count two.

views.christian: Catholic and Orthodox: seven sacraments; the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. Lutheran: Christ is truly present. Reformed: a spiritual presence. Baptist: a memorial. Most churches baptise infants; Baptists and Pentecostals baptise believers only.
views.muslim: Islam has no sacraments. Ritual washing before prayer (wudu) and full washing (ghusl) are acts of purity, not of salvation.
views.jewish: Immersion in a ritual bath (mikveh) is used for purity and conversion; there are no sacraments in the Christian sense.

refs: This is my body; this cup is the new covenant in my blood.
Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man.
[[go/trent-canons-and-decrees/Session XIII › Sacrament of the Eucharist|Trent on the Eucharist]]
Lutheran teaching on baptism and the Supper.

topics.title: Saints, icons and images
topics.summary: Orthodox and Catholics venerate saints and images; Protestants, Muslims and Jews reject prayer to saints and religious images, though Shia Muslims visit the shrines of the Imams.

views.christian: Orthodox and Catholic: saints are asked to pray for us and icons are venerated, not worshipped. Protestants: pray to God alone, through Christ.
views.muslim: Worship belongs to God alone; images of living beings are discouraged and idolatry is the gravest sin. Many Sunnis reject seeking help at tombs; Shia visit shrines of the Imams.
views.jewish: No images of God and no prayer to intermediaries.

refs: You shall not make a carved image.
Cherubim made for the ark: cited by those who defend images.
One mediator between God and men.
God does not forgive associating partners with him.
We only worship them to bring us nearer to God.
[[go/trent-canons-and-decrees/Session XXV › Invocation, Veneration, and on Relics of Saints and Sacred Images|Trent on saints and images]]

topics.title: Forgiveness and repentance
topics.summary: All three faiths teach that God forgives the repentant. Christianity grounds forgiveness in the cross; Islam and Judaism in God's mercy and a person's sincere return to God.

views.christian: Forgiveness is offered through Christ's death. Believers must forgive others as they are forgiven. Catholics and Orthodox confess to a priest.
views.muslim: God is the Most Merciful and forgives all sins to the one who sincerely repents, except dying while associating partners with God.
views.jewish: Repentance (teshuvah), prayer and charity bring forgiveness; Yom Kippur atones for sins against God, but wrongs against people need their forgiveness first.

refs: If we confess our sins, he is faithful to forgive.
Forgive others, and your Father will forgive you.
If the wicked turns, he shall live.
As far as the east is from the west.
Do not despair of God's mercy; he forgives all sins.
God will change their evil deeds into good.

topics.title: Love, enemies and the golden rule
topics.summary: All three faiths command love of neighbour and some form of the golden rule. Jesus' “love your enemies” is the most radical form.

views.christian: Love God and neighbour, love even enemies, turn the other cheek, do to others as you would have them do to you.
views.muslim: None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Repel evil with what is better. Justice even toward those you hate.
views.jewish: Love your neighbour as yourself. Hillel: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; that is the whole Torah.

refs: Turn the other cheek; love your enemies.
Repel evil with what is better.
Do not let hatred of a people make you unjust.
Love for your brother what you love for yourself.
Hillel: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow.

topics.title: War and violence in scripture
topics.summary: All three scriptures contain war. Each tradition reads its war passages in context and limits them, and critics on every side point to the others' texts.

views.christian: The wars of ancient Israel were for one people at one time. Jesus refused the sword and taught love of enemies. Christian tradition later developed the just-war theory.
views.muslim: Fighting is allowed in self-defence and against oppression, within strict limits: no aggression, no harm to non-combatants, peace when the enemy seeks peace. Jihad first means striving against one's own evil.
views.jewish: The commands of conquest applied to nations that no longer exist and cannot be applied today; the rabbis limited the laws of war.

refs: Offer peace first; the special case of the Canaanites.
All who take the sword will perish by the sword.
The ruler does not bear the sword in vain.
Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.
The “sword verse”, about those who broke treaties.
If they incline to peace, incline to it.
Whoever kills a soul, it is as if he killed all mankind.
Whoever saves one life saves a whole world.

topics.title: Women
topics.summary: All three scriptures were written in societies led by men, and all contain passages praised for honouring women and passages criticised as restricting them. Each tradition reads them in different ways today.

views.christian: Men and women are equal before God. Churches differ on women's roles: Catholics and Orthodox ordain only men; many Protestant churches ordain women.
views.muslim: Men and women are equal in faith and reward, with different roles and rights in family law. Muslims point out that Islam gave women inheritance and property rights in 7th-century Arabia.
views.jewish: Orthodox Judaism gives men and women different religious duties; Reform and Conservative Judaism ordain women as rabbis.

refs: Male and female he created them, in his image.
Neither male nor female; all one in Christ.
A woman should learn in silence: debated today.
Wives submit; husbands love as Christ loved the church.
Believing men and believing women, the same reward.
Men as protectors of women: much debated.

topics.title: Marriage, divorce and polygamy
topics.summary: All three faiths honour marriage. Islam allows up to four wives under conditions; Judaism once allowed several, and Christianity teaches one man and one woman. Their rules on divorce differ.

views.christian: Marriage is a lifelong covenant of one man and one woman. Jesus forbade divorce except for unfaithfulness; the Catholic Church does not recognise divorce, while Orthodox and Protestants allow it in some cases.
views.muslim: Marriage is strongly encouraged. A man may marry up to four wives if he treats them justly. Divorce is permitted but disliked.
views.jewish: Marriage is a holy duty. Divorce is permitted with a bill of divorce (get). Polygamy was banned among European Jews about a thousand years ago.

refs: The two shall become one flesh.
I hate divorce, says the LORD.
What God has joined, let no one separate.
Marry two, three or four; if you fear injustice, then one.
You will not be able to be fully just between wives.
He placed love and mercy between you.

topics.title: Angels, Satan and jinn
topics.summary: All three faiths believe in angels. Christians and Muslims believe in Satan as a fallen being; Islam adds the jinn. Judaism often sees Satan as an accuser serving God.

views.christian: Angels are God's messengers; Satan is a fallen angel defeated by Christ.
views.muslim: Angels are made of light and always obey. Iblis was a jinn who refused to bow to Adam. Jinn are beings made of fire, some believers and some not.
views.jewish: Angels carry out God's will. The satan (“accuser”) in Job tests people with God's permission.

refs: Paul's thorn, a messenger of Satan.
A group of jinn listened to the Quran.

topics.title: Creation
topics.summary: All three faiths teach that God created the world from nothing and made humans. The Bible and Quran both speak of six days and of Adam; believers differ on how literally to read them.

views.christian: God created everything good. Many Christians read Genesis literally; many others accept an old universe and evolution guided by God.
views.muslim: God created the heavens and the earth in six periods. Adam was made from clay and taught the names; humanity is God's trustee (khalifa) on earth.
views.jewish: The creation story teaches that one God made a good world and every person in his image. Jewish thinkers have long read it on several levels.

refs: All things were made through the Word.
Created the heavens and earth in six days.
Adam, God's trustee, is taught the names.
The heavens and earth were joined, and We split them.

topics.title: Fate and free will
topics.summary: All three faiths hold that God knows and rules everything and that people are responsible for their choices. They differ on how the two fit.

views.christian: Calvinists: God chose whom to save. Arminians, Methodists, Catholics and Orthodox: grace is offered to all and can be refused.
views.muslim: Sunnis count belief in God's decree (qadar) as an article of faith; people still choose and are judged. Shia stress God's justice and human free will.
views.jewish: Rabbi Akiva: everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given.

refs: Jacob I loved, Esau I hated; the potter and the clay.
Chosen before the foundation of the world.
God desires all people to be saved.
We created everything according to a measure.
The hadith of Gabriel: belief in the decree, good and bad.

topics.title: Slavery
topics.summary: The Bible and Quran both regulate slavery, which existed everywhere when they were written. Both also encourage freeing slaves. All three faiths today reject slavery, and critics ask why the texts did not ban it outright.

views.christian: Christians point to the Exodus, Paul's appeal for Onesimus and “neither slave nor free” as seeds of abolition; Christian abolitionists led the campaign to end slavery.
views.muslim: Islam restricted slavery and made freeing slaves an act of great merit and an atonement for sins, a path Muslims say was meant to end it.
views.jewish: The Torah limited Hebrew servitude to six years and remembers that Israel were slaves in Egypt.

refs: Hebrew servants go free in the seventh year.
Do not return an escaped slave.
No longer a slave, but a beloved brother.
The steep path: freeing a slave.
Grant a contract of freedom to those who seek it.
Freeing a believing slave as atonement.

topics.title: Salvation for people of other faiths
topics.summary: Each faith has strict and generous voices on whether outsiders can be saved.

views.christian: Jesus said no one comes to the Father but through him. Some Christians hold that only those who believe in Christ are saved; others, including Catholic teaching since the 1960s, hold that God's grace can reach people outside the Church.
views.muslim: The Quran praises some Jews and Christians who believe in God and do good, and also says that whoever seeks a religion other than Islam will not have it accepted. Scholars differ on how these fit.
views.jewish: Non-Jews need not become Jews; the righteous of all nations, who keep the seven laws of Noah, have a share in the World to Come.

refs: No one comes to the Father except through me.
No other name under heaven by which we must be saved.
In every nation, whoever fears him is acceptable.
Gentiles who do by nature what the law requires.
Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe and do good will have their reward.
Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will not be accepted.
Argue with the People of the Book in the best way.
The seven laws given to the descendants of Noah.

topics.title: Suffering and evil
topics.summary: All three faiths wrestle with why a good God allows suffering. Each sees trials as a test and points to justice beyond this life.

views.christian: God brings good out of evil and shares in human suffering on the cross; one day he will wipe away every tear.
views.muslim: Life is a test; patience in hardship is rewarded, and nothing happens without God's knowledge and wisdom.
views.jewish: The book of Job refuses easy answers. Suffering can call us to repentance and to faithfulness, and God's justice is not always visible in this world.

refs: The LORD gave and the LORD has taken away.
Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?
All things work together for good.
My power is made perfect in weakness.
He will wipe away every tear.
We will test you; give good news to the patient.
God burdens no soul beyond its capacity.
He created death and life to test you.

topics.title: Circumcision
topics.summary: Circumcision is the sign of the covenant in Judaism and a normal practice in Islam. The early Church ruled that non-Jewish Christians need not be circumcised.

views.christian: Not required: the apostles ruled against it for non-Jewish believers, and Paul speaks of “circumcision of the heart”.
views.muslim: Part of the natural way (fitra) followed since Abraham; most scholars consider it strongly recommended or required for men.
views.jewish: The covenant of Abraham, performed on the eighth day.

refs: Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything.
Five practices of the fitra, including circumcision.

topics.title: Pilgrimage and holy places
topics.summary: Mecca is Islam's holiest city and the goal of the hajj. Jerusalem is holy to all three faiths: the Temple for Jews, the places of Jesus' death and resurrection for Christians, and al-Aqsa for Muslims.

views.christian: Pilgrimage to the holy places is a devotion, not a duty; worship is “in spirit and truth”, not tied to one place.
views.muslim: The hajj to Mecca is required once in a lifetime for those able. Jerusalem's al-Aqsa is the third holiest site.
views.jewish: Jerusalem and the Temple Mount are the holiest places; Jews pray toward Jerusalem and long for the Temple to be rebuilt.

refs: Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD.
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem.
Not on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth.
The first house at Bakka; pilgrimage is a duty for those able.
Turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.
The night journey to the farthest mosque.

topics.title: Prophets
topics.summary: All three faiths believe God spoke through prophets. They agree on many of the same figures, from Abraham to Moses, but disagree about Jesus and Muhammad.

views.christian: God spoke through the prophets and finally through his Son; Jesus is more than a prophet.
views.muslim: God sent prophets to every nation, from Adam to Muhammad, the last. All prophets taught the same faith and are protected from grave sin.
views.jewish: Prophecy ended with Malachi; Moses is the greatest prophet. Neither Jesus nor Muhammad is accepted.

refs: God spoke through the prophets, and now by his Son.
How to recognise a true prophet.
The last words of the prophets.
We sent a messenger to every nation.
We make no distinction between any of his messengers.

topics.title: Who is God? Names and nature of God
topics.summary: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all worship the one God of Abraham. Whether they worship “the same God” is debated, mainly because of the Trinity. Arab Christians also call God “Allah”.

views.christian: God is one, revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and God is love. Many Christians say Muslims and Jews worship the same God but know him incompletely; others disagree.
views.muslim: Allah is the one God, the same God who sent Abraham, Moses and Jesus, known through his ninety-nine names.
views.jewish: The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whose personal name (YHWH) is not pronounced; one, without body or form.

refs: Merciful and gracious, slow to anger.
Our God and your God is one.

topics.title: Hard passages and the Old Testament
topics.summary: Many readers are troubled by Old Testament passages on war, punishment and the treatment of women. Christians and Jews have several ways of reading them.

views.christian: Describing is not approving; Jesus is the lens; ancient context; God's judgment on grave evils; and gradual revelation.
views.muslim: Many Muslims hold that the present Torah is not fully preserved, so not every story is an accurate record of what the prophets did.
views.jewish: The rabbis read these texts through centuries of interpretation that limits them, and some commentators wrestle openly with their moral difficulty.

refs: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
Because of the hardness of your hearts.
You have heard … but I say to you.

topics.title: Who was Jesus?
topics.summary: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher in first-century Galilee and Judea who was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Christians worship him as the Son of God; Muslims honour him as the Messiah and a great prophet; Jews do not accept him as the Messiah.

views.christian: Jesus is God the Son who became man, born of the Virgin Mary. He taught, healed, forgave sins, died on the cross for the world and rose on the third day. He will return to judge the living and the dead.
views.muslim: Isa son of Maryam is one of the greatest messengers, born of a virgin, given the Gospel, and a worker of miracles by God's permission. He was not God and was not crucified, but was raised to God and will return.
views.jewish: Jesus was a Jew of his time. He is not the Messiah, since the messianic age has not come, and not a prophet or divine.

refs: The Sermon on the Mount begins.
“Who do you say that I am?”
His birth announced, and his miracles.

topics.title: King David
topics.summary: David is the shepherd who killed Goliath and became Israel's greatest king. Jews honour him as the ancestor of the Messiah and the author of many Psalms; Christians as the ancestor of Jesus; Muslims as a prophet-king who received the Psalms (Zabur).

views.christian: God promised David an everlasting throne; Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus, the “Son of David”. David's sin with Bathsheba and his repentance are a model of confession.
views.muslim: Dawud is a prophet and king to whom God gave the Zabur and wisdom. Muslim scholars generally reject the story of adultery with Bathsheba as unworthy of a prophet.
views.jewish: David is the ideal king and the ancestor of the Messiah, who will come from his line. Tradition credits him with much of the book of Psalms.

refs: God's promise of an everlasting throne.
Peter applies David's psalm to Jesus.
David, God's vicegerent, and the two disputants.

topics.title: Noah and the flood
topics.summary: All three faiths tell of Noah, the righteous man saved from the flood. Judaism draws from his story the seven laws for all humanity; Christians see the flood as judgment and a picture of baptism; the Quran presents Noah as a messenger whose people, and even his son, rejected him.

views.christian: The flood shows God's judgment on sin and his mercy to the righteous; the New Testament compares it to baptism and to the coming of the Son of Man.
views.muslim: Nuh is one of the great messengers. He called his people to God for 950 years; they mocked him, and his own son refused to board the ark and drowned.
views.jewish: After the flood God made a covenant with all humanity. The rabbis derive from it the seven laws of Noah, by which the righteous of every nation have a share in the World to Come.

refs: The flood announced and the ark built.
As in the days of Noah.
He remained among them a thousand years less fifty.
The seven laws of the descendants of Noah.
